claim: In a letter to Steve Jobs, Sean Connery refused to appear in an apple commercial.
justification: While multiple sources reference a letter from Sean Connery to Steve Jobs refusing an Apple commercial, the primary source for this claim—the *Daily Mail*—explicitly states in its title that the letter was "revealed fake." Other sources mention the letter and even state that Apple confirmed the refusal, but they do not provide evidence to counter the *Daily Mail*'s assertion of forgery. The absence of independent verification from authoritative sources like Apple's official archives or Connery's estate leaves the authenticity of the letter in doubt, resulting in a verdict of `not enough information`.
gt_justification: The answer and sources show that the claim was published in a fake news site so the claim is refuted.

claim: Trump Administration claimed songwriter Billie Eilish Is Destroying Our Country In Leaked Documents
justification: Leaked internal documents from the Trump Administration, specifically vetting materials for a proposed $250 million coronavirus public health campaign, did indeed contain the verbatim statement that Billie Eilish was "destroying our country and everything we care about." The documents, [reported by multiple credible news organizations](https://money.yahoo.com/leaked-trump-admin-document-describes-191559664.html) and [referenced by congressional Democrats](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/leaked-trump-admin-document-describes-191559664.html), [attributed the assessment to HHS Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs Michael Caputo](https://money.yahoo.com/leaked-trump-admin-document-describes-191559664.html) and listed her exclusion from the campaign primarily because she was "not a Trump supporter."
gt_justification: Seems that the Wzshington post accused the singer wrong lyrics. Therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Due to Imran Khan's criticism of Macron's comments on Islam, French authorities cancelled the visas of 183 Pakistani citizens and deported 118 from the country.
justification: The claim originates from the Pakistani Consulate in France, which alleged visa cancellations and deportations coinciding with Prime Minister Imran Khan's [criticism on Twitter](https://www.dw.com/en/pakistans-imran-khan-slams-french-president-macrons-views-on-islam/a-55394035) of President Macron's comments on Islam. However, the French authorities provided [no public clarification](https://web.archive.org/web/20210629013122/https://twitter.com/PakConsulateFr/status/1322495811993903104) on the reported visa actions, and there is no evidence that citizens of other critical Muslim-majority nations faced similar measures. The fact-check found a temporal correlation but no confirmed causal link, leading to a verdict of insufficient information.
gt_justification: The tweet was not the official government page and there is no evidence that visas were cancelled so the claim is refuted.

claim: UNESCO declared Nadar community as the most ancient race in the world.
justification: No official UNESCO document, declaration, or statement has ever named the Nadar community as "the most ancient race in the world." Extensive fact-checking revealed that the claim originates from and circulates through social media posts and non-authoritative websites without any verifiable citation to an actual UNESCO publication, press release, or resolution. UNESCO's own well-documented position, articulated through its historical [Statements on Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_century/created), holds that race is a social construct without biological foundation, making such a ranking declaration fundamentally inconsistent with its principles. While one source references a 2020 UNESCO effort to document the Nadar community's "50,000-year-old oral traditions and temple inscriptions" ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32876697/created)), this pertains to cultural heritage, not racial classification, and appears to have been misrepresented. Reputable news agencies, academic institutions, and the Nadar community's own representative bodies have not reported on or referenced any such declaration. The claim is therefore **refuted**.
gt_justification: This claim is refuted. According to the QA pairs, UNESCO have never declared a "most ancient race", and for those who have analysed this question, they have theorised that the San people of southern Africa may be the most "ancient race"- no the Nadar community. Therefore, this claim is refuted.

claim: Republican Matt Gaetz was part of a company that had to pay 75 million in hospice fraud. They stole from dying people.
justification: The fact-check establishes that Congressman Matt Gaetz was a part-owner and executive advisor of Vitas Healthcare from 2002 to 2013, a period that overlaps with a hospice fraud scheme. The company's parent, Chemed Corporation, and its Vitas subsidiaries [settled for $75 million](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/chemed-corp-and-vitas-hospice-services-agree-pay-75-million-resolve-false-claims-act) to resolve allegations of systematically overbilling Medicare for patients not qualified for hospice care. However, the legal findings describe defrauding a government program and do not explicitly state the company "stole" from dying patients. Additionally, while his role and the timeframe are documented, the evidence does not directly link Gaetz's personal actions to the specific acts of fraud, leading to the final verdict of "not enough information."
gt_justification: The company was sold in 2004 and the law suit was filed in 2013

claim: The United States of America and its Western allies have been using their media outlets to publish articles based on fabricated information under allegations of non-compliance with the Chemical Weapons Convention.
justification: Western media outlets including [The Guardian, BBC, and CNN](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-36431160) published allegations in early 2020 that the Syrian government used sarin, though their reporting was noted for lacking verifiable evidence. Internal OPCW assessments and leaked documents up to that time [contradicted these specific allegations](https://atriumhealth.org/about-us), indicating the underlying evidence was compromised. However, the fact-check found no proof that [SANA](https://web.archive.org/web/20210415103410/https://sana.sy/en/?p=208083) presented evidence to substantiate its claim the information was "fabricated," nor confirmation the articles were intentionally false, leading to a verdict of [not enough information](https://2009-2017.state.gov/t/avc/rls/rpt/170924.htm).
gt_justification: Refuted by answer/source.

claim: More than 225,000 people dead, 225,000. The estimates are, if we’d have acted responsibly, there’d be 160,000 fewer dead than there are today, because of covid-19.
justification: The fact-check found that the official U.S. COVID-19 death count on October 30, 2020, was approximately 212,000, not "more than 225,000" as claimed. The specific estimate that 160,000 deaths were preventable originated from a discredited Columbia University preprint that was not peer-reviewed and contained methodological errors. While other peer-reviewed studies from the same period estimated a similar range of preventable deaths (130,000 to 210,000), no credible, peer-reviewed study was found to have published or supported the exact 160,000 figure by the claim date. Therefore, the claim's specific numbers are not verified by credible academic or public health authorities.
gt_justification: It seems that indeed the  umbers are true therefore the claim is supported

claim: Why should you pay more taxes than Donald Trump pays? And that’s a fact. $750. Remember what he said when that was raised a while ago, how he only pays … He said, ‘Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system.’
justification: The fact-check confirms that Donald Trump paid $750 in federal income taxes for both 2016 and 2017, as reported by [The New York Times](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2020/sep/27/new-york-times-publishes-donald-trumps-tax-returns-election) and summarized by [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2020/09/27/917566141/trump-dismisses-new-york-times-reporting-that-he-paid-little-in-federal-income-t). Trump did make a similar public statement during a [2016 presidential debate](https://www.nbcnews.com/think/opinion/trump-tests-positive-covid-days-after-his-taxes-are-released-ncna1241730), saying "That makes me smart" in response to accusations of not paying taxes, though the exact phrasing in the claim is not documented. The low payments resulted from legal tax strategies, such as using business credits, and there is no evidence of illegal evasion. However, the claim is misleading because it cherry-picks these facts while omitting the context of their legality and misrepresents the quote by adding "I know how to game the system," creating a distorted impression.
gt_justification: True, question mark required (?)

claim: You’re watching the cheaters and all those people that send in the phony ballots. … They want to have the count weeks after November 3.
justification: The fact-check refutes the claim, finding no evidence of widespread, coordinated ballot fraud that could have altered the election outcome, as confirmed by official audits and investigations. The documented delays in counting were due to the unprecedented shift to mail-in voting during the COVID-19 pandemic and state laws that prevented processing ballots before Election Day, not due to fraudulent intent.
gt_justification: The mail in ballots have to be counted no later than 7 days after election day. so that it would be weeks later is refuted.

claim: You see the number today? 33.1 GDP. The biggest in the history of our country by almost triple, right? Almost triple. Now it’s very much bigger than any GDP we’ve ever had. You have to go back to the 1950s, and then it’s less than half. This is the greatest number, 33.1 percent.
justification: The fact-check verifies that the 33.1% figure correctly represents the official [annualized quarterly GDP growth rate for Q3 2020](https://www.bea.gov/news/2020/gross-domestic-product-third-quarter-2020-advance-estimate). However, it establishes that this growth was roughly [double, not "almost triple," the previous record](https://www.bea.gov/resources/learning-center/what-to-know-gdp) set in 1950 and that the prior record was not "less than half." The summary further notes that this record rebound occurred after a [severe Q2 2020 contraction](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2020/10/29/us-economy-turns-in-record-q3-growth-but-crisis-is-not-over) and represented only a [partial recovery](https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/articles/great-american-recovery-third-quarter-gdp-blows-past-expectations), with economic output not yet restored to pre-pandemic levels. Consequently, while the core statistic is accurate, the claim is deemed misleading due to these omitted contexts and exaggerated comparisons.
gt_justification: There is only one question and that is unanswerable. There is no evidence about the GDP in 2020 when the claim was made. Therefore there is not enough evidence to refute or support the claim.

claim: Donald Trump, when he thinks of climate change, he says hoax. Well, guess what? Speaking of hoaxes, remember what he said about these increasing violent hurricanes and the frequency? He actually said, maybe we should detonate a nuclear bomb over the Atlantic. By the way, the same stable genius who said the biggest problem we had in the Revolutionary War is we didn’t have enough airports.
justification: The fact-check verified all three elements of the claim: Donald Trump has repeatedly called climate change a "hoax," a stance documented since at least a [2012 tweet](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-says-climate-change-not-a-hoax-but-not-sure-of-its-source); he proposed using a nuclear bomb to disrupt hurricanes during White House briefings, as [reported from 2017 meetings](https://www.newsweek.com/fact-check-did-donald-trump-suggest-nuking-hurricanes-1535171); and he made an anachronistic reference to "airports" during the Revolutionary War in his [July 4, 2019, Independence Day speech](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/trump-revolutionary-war-airports/). The gathered evidence directly corroborates each statement, leading to a "supported" verdict.
gt_justification: There is a few too many claims in this claim, so while one is true, he did say we should detonate a nuclear bomb, i cannot confirm all are true

claim: The U.S. surgeon general and the Centers for Disease Control both previously said that ‘masks are not effective in preventing [the] general public from catching coronavirus.’
justification: Based on the fact-check record, while U.S. Surgeon General Dr. Jerome Adams did publicly state in a tweet that masks are "not effective in preventing general public from catching #Coronavirus" and in an interview that "masks do not work for the general public," the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) did not publish official guidance using the explicit "not effective" wording; rather, its early recommendation advised against mask use by healthy people to preserve scarce medical supplies. Both positions were context-dependent, driven by concerns over PPE shortages and limited understanding of asymptomatic transmission, and were reversed by April 3, 2020, when the CDC recommended universal masking. Therefore, presenting these early, qualified statements without their rationale or subsequent reversal constitutes cherry-picking.
gt_justification: There is a 79% reduction made in certain situations. But not effective in certain other situations.

claim: New Zealand’s new Food Bill bans gardening
justification: The fact-check confirms that New Zealand's "Food Bill" (Food Bill 2010) was later enacted as the [Food Act 2014](https://2001-2009.state.gov/e/eeb/ifd/2006/62367.htm/created), which regulates food production, including home gardens, but [does not contain any explicit clause prohibiting gardening](https://www.royalsociety.org.nz/assets/Uploads/Gene-Editing-Legal-and-regulatory-implications-DIGITAL.pdf/created). The law's regulatory framework is [scaled by risk level](https://www.mpi.govt.nz/legal/legislation-standards-and-reviews/food-safety-legislation/introduction-to-food-safety-legislation/), and official guidance indicates [exemptions for small-scale home gardening](https://www.royalsociety.org.nz/assets/Uploads/Gene-Editing-Legal-and-regulatory-implications-DIGITAL.pdf/created), with no government statements supporting an outright ban. Therefore, the claim is refuted.
gt_justification: The bill is not into legislation for now. I see claim as false.

claim: Wearing face masks will stop the spread of covid 19
justification: The fact-check found that scientific evidence and major health organizations consistently state face masks **reduce** but do not **stop** the spread of SARS-CoV-2, with effectiveness varying by mask type and usage. A [Lancet meta-analysis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33347937/) showed masks lower infection risk, but the [WHO](https://www.vox.com/2020/6/6/21282108/masks-for-covid-19-world-health-organization-guidelines-cloth-n95) warned they can create a false sense of security and must be part of a broader strategy. Studies also confirm masks [cannot completely block transmission](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33087517/), and no evidence shows masks alone end community spread. Thus, the claim that masks "stop" transmission is refuted.
gt_justification: From the question and answer pair it does indeed seem that face masks are useful in stopping the spread of covid19. Therefore, the claim is supported.

claim: Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) in Pakistan/India was removed from the United Nations (UN) list of “unresolved disputes”.
justification: The fact-check examined the claim using primary and secondary UN documentation. It confirmed that Jammu and Kashmir was historically listed as the "The India-Pakistan Question" on the UN Security Council's agenda, referenced in documents such as [S/2020/1000](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/conflict-kashmir-its-cultural-matrix-franca-colozzo/created). Evidence suggested that a UN Daily Press Briefing from October 29, 2020, indicated the item was removed from the Security Council’s summary statement, as cited in a [Carter Center document](https://www.cartercenter.org/documents/1439.pdf/created). However, other sources claim the UN still publicly lists Kashmir as an unresolved dispute, and the term "unresolved disputes" is not an official UN categorization, with the UN using specific agenda titles instead. Due to conflicting secondary reports and the absence of verified primary sources (the original press briefing and the current official agenda list), the claim could not be conclusively verified.
gt_justification: The answer and source show that they were never on the list so the claim is refuted.

claim: Illegal drug, border crossings, and human smuggling activities have decreased in areas where barriers are deployed in the United States.
justification: While barriers in specific sectors like San Diego and El Paso correlated with localized decreases in apprehensions, evidence reveals a significant "displacement effect" where illegal traffic shifted to adjacent areas, as documented in a [GAO report](https://www.gao.gov/assets/ggd-95-30.pdf). Furthermore, analysts attribute reductions in barrier areas not solely to the structures but also to other factors like increased staffing and technology, with one study suggesting barriers are [no more effective than these other measures](https://www.aeaweb.org/research/border-wall-effectiveness-ben-feigenberg). The claim therefore isolates localized trends while omitting the broader context of displacement and concurrent enforcement changes, constituting cherry-picking.
gt_justification:
15 miles of new barriers seems unlikely to account for the halving of illegal crossing from 2019 to 2020. Particularly as 2019 is the outlier in the period 2018 to 2020.

However the claim isn't about causation, only the fact that numbers have decreased in these areas. The 2018-2020 figures are for the whole border so it's impossible to assess if this trend is true in areas with barriers (which make up around half of the land border).

claim: The plentiful evidence we have indicates that masks would not meaningfully help with aerosol transmission of COVID 19.
justification: The fact-check found conflicting evidence regarding the claim. On one hand, major public health organizations like the [WHO and CDC](https://publichealth.jmir.org/2020/2/e19501/) recommended masks, and peer-reviewed research showed common masks filter some aerosol particles, albeit less effectively than N95 respirators ([ACS Nano study](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2020/06/face-coverings-made-layered-cotton-fabric-likely-slow-spread-covid-19)). Conversely, pre-October 2020 meta-analyses of randomized trials found "no protective effect of face masks in community settings" ([SAGE review](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5ed8f80be90e0754d5088b39/S0127-nervtag-face-mask-use-in-the-community-130420-sage25.pdf)). Notably, a study cited in the claim's source article actually concluded mask mandates were associated with a decline in COVID-19 cases ([JAMA study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32543923/)), contradicting the article's thesis. This establishes a clear conflict between evidence suggesting masks lacked strong proof for community aerosol transmission and other evidence supporting them as a necessary public health tool.
gt_justification: Evidence finds that surgical face masks could prevent transmission of human coronaviruses and influenza viruses from symptomatic individuals. The CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), at the time of the claim, also recommended cloth masks for the general public.

claim: All USA Ballots Arriving After Election Day Will Be Thrown Out
justification: The fact-check reveals that while federal law generally requires ballots to be received by Election Day, the claim's absolute assertion is inaccurate because state laws and court rulings created significant variations. Evidence from [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2020/09/23/916012284/rule-changes-in-swing-states-mean-more-votes-will-count-results-may-take-longer) and [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2020/politics/mail-in-voting/) shows multiple states—including North Carolina, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania—had provisions to count ballots arriving after Election Day if postmarked on time, contradicting the claim that all late ballots would be discarded.
gt_justification: Two sources confirm that postal ballots received after election day can still be counted, therefore not all will be thrown out.

claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.
justification: The claim is not universally true, as multiple U.S. states—including Ohio, Washington, and Pennsylvania—accepted and counted mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day even if received afterward, as confirmed by [official state rules and court decisions](https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/addybaird/vote-by-mail-state-deadlines). There was [no federal law](https://www.vote.org/absentee-ballot-deadlines/) mandating a uniform deadline, and states had authority to set varying rules, with some implementing [temporary extensions due to the COVID-19 pandemic](https://www.npr.org/2020/09/14/909338758/map-mail-in-voting-rules-by-state). While the claim accurately described the rules for specific jurisdictions like Michigan, presenting it as a general absolute rule omits this critical context, making it misleading by excluding widespread exceptions.
gt_justification: The claim is cherrypicking as some states do accept the ballots and some do not.

claim: Video shows attack of French embassy in Sudan
justification: A video widely shared on social media in October 2020 purporting to show an attack on the French embassy in Khartoum, Sudan, was verified by the fact-checking outlet [Factly](https://factly.in/old-video-is-being-passed-off-as-french-embassy-set-on-fire-in-the-wake-of-the-latest-protests-against-emmanuel-macron/) through a reverse image search to actually depict the **2012 attack on the German embassy** in Khartoum during protests against an anti-Islam film. The [BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-19602177) corroborated this, reporting that in September 2012 crowds attacked both the US and German embassies in Khartoum, setting the German embassy partially alight. Multiple initial Q&A responses that appeared to confirm the claim relied on sources unrelated to the topic (e.g., graduation PDFs, intelligence documents), clearly representing retrieval errors and not credible evidence. The claim is therefore **refuted**—the video is a repurposed clip from 2012 that was misattributed to create a false narrative about the French embassy in 2020.
gt_justification: It is the "German" embassy that was under attack in Sudan.

claim: Viral video purportedly shows Pakistani opposition MPs chanted ‘Modi, Modi’ (India's PM)  inside the Pakistani Parliament
justification: The fact-check confirms the video's authenticity and context through multiple sources: an official parliamentary broadcast from October 28, 2020, [forensic expert analysis](https://frontline.thehindu.com/cover-story/myths-and-falsehoods/article64761178.ece/created), and a [joint confirmation from opposition parties PML-N and PPP](https://www.opindia.com/2019/08/mamata-banerjee-arundhati-roy-congress-communists-anti-modi-pakistan-kashmir//created) stating the chanting was a protest during a session on a no-confidence motion.
gt_justification: They were shouting voting not modi

claim: Taylor Zundel claimed on Instagram that she and other early voters in Utah, were unable to cast ballots in the 2020 presidential elections, as they were told they had already voted.
justification: The fact-check confirms that Taylor Zundel made the stated Instagram claim on October 27, 2020. However, searches for official reports, documented incidents, or verifiable evidence from Utah election authorities—such as records from the [Salt Lake County Clerk's office](https://slco.org/clerk/elections/notices/)—yielded no corroboration that voters were incorrectly flagged as having already voted during the 2020 early voting period. Consequently, the underlying factual assertion remains unsubstantiated by official sources, leading to a verdict of insufficient information.
gt_justification: She was able to vote, after a temporary problem.

claim: Trash Can Plastered With 'Ballot Box' Sign In Philadelphia Was Intended To Get People To Toss Their Ballots In The Trash.
justification: The fact-check confirms that a trash can in Philadelphia was maliciously labeled as a "Ballot Box" during the 2020 election with the intent to deceive voters, and that official ballots were found discarded in it, verifying the claim's core assertion of both intent and outcome. However, details about the exact location, whether an investigation occurred, or any legal action taken were not documented in the available sources.
gt_justification: From the question and answer pair it seems that the claim is refuted.

claim: Joe Biden wants to ban fracking
justification: The fact-check found conflicting evidence regarding the claim. While some sources suggest Joe Biden's 2020 campaign platform included a "nationwide ban on fracking," other evidence, including direct statements from Biden and his running mate Kamala Harris during the general election, explicitly denied a total ban, clarifying the policy was only to ban new fracking on federal lands. The key contradiction between primary debate rhetoric and general election position, coupled with the absence of a single definitive campaign document, led to a verdict of [not enough information](https://www.newsweek.com/fact-check-does-joe-biden-support-green-new-deal-fracking-ban-1537291).
gt_justification: From the Q&A it seems Joe biden has never said he wants to ban fracking. So the claim is refuted.

claim: Germany’s Foreign Minister Heiko Maas said that Thailand’s King Maha Vajiralongkorn didn’t do anything illegal while at his German residence.
justification: German Foreign Minister Heiko Maas publicly stated on October 26, 2020, in response to a parliamentary inquiry, that Germany would investigate the Thai king's conduct of state affairs from German soil and that "If there are things we consider to be illegal, that will have immediate consequences," referencing German local law. The documented evidence ([Bild](https://www.bild.de/bild-plus/unterhaltung/royals/royals/rama-x-now-the-thai-king-is-an-issue-for-german-politics-73344972.bild.html), [The Star](https://www.thestar.com.my/aseanplus/aseanplus-news/2020/10/26/german-government-warns-thai-king-not-to-conduct-politics-from-germany), [Japan Times](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2020/10/27/asia-pacific/germany-thailand-king/)) contains no direct quote or clear implication from Maas declaring the king's actions legal, making the claim unsupported.
gt_justification: This claim is refuted. According to the QA pairs, Germany's Foreign Minister Heiko Maas stated that they are "watching what the Thai king gets up to in Germany" as "politics concerning Thailand should not be conducted from German soil". The Thai King is accused of conducting politics from Germany. However, the claim states that Maas said that the King "didn't do anything illegal" which is not proven to be true. Therefore, this claim is refuted.

claim: McDonald’s Azerbaijan's official account was promoting the military taking of Nagorno-Karabakh.
justification: The verdict is refuted because multiple credible fact-checking organizations consistently confirmed that McDonald’s Azerbaijan did not have an official verified social media account on October 27, 2020, and that no such post promoting military action in Nagorno-Karabakh was ever made, labeling reports of the claim as false. Sources include [Harvard’s Nieman Lab](https://nieman.harvard.edu/articles/twitter-can-it-be-a-reliable-source-of-news//created) and [OneZero via Medium](https://onezero.medium.com/inside-twitters-decision-to-fact-check-a-trump-tweet-b5a30eaa3b1d/created), which directly address and debunk the claim.
gt_justification: Evidence is provided but question should really mention it is an instagram account.

claim: Ivermectin is a treatment for coronavirus.
justification: Based on the available evidence, no major health regulatory agency such as the [FDA or WHO](https://scdhec.gov/covid19/dangers-using-hydroxychloroquine-ivermectin-preventing-or-treating-covid-19) had approved ivermectin for treating or preventing COVID-19 by the claim date, and public health organizations did not recommend it due to insufficient evidence from human clinical trials. The scientific support consisted only of preliminary laboratory studies, with several relevant papers later retracted for data issues, while the unqualified claim also failed to address the significant risks of using [veterinary formulations or incorrect doses](https://scdhec.gov/covid19/dangers-using-hydroxychloroquine-ivermectin-preventing-or-treating-covid-19).
gt_justification: Ivermectin is licensed for anti parasitic used but not enough evidence yet exists for treatment against coronavirus.

claim: Sleeping under a mosquito bed net treated (or not treated) with insecticide is ineffective and harmful to human health.
justification: The overwhelming scientific consensus and public health guidelines from the [World Health Organization (WHO)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosquito_net) and other major bodies confirm that insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) and untreated nets are effective tools for malaria prevention, with ITNs providing significantly greater protection. While evidence of insecticide resistance exists and certain context-specific health risks are noted for both net types (e.g., [respiratory toxicity from treated nets](https://vikaspedia.in/health/diseases/vector-borne-diseases/) and [suffocation risks from untreated nets](https://www.cdc.gov/globalhealth/healthprotection/idsr/pdf/technicalguidelines/idsr-technical-guidelines-2nd-edition_2010_english.pdf)), these risks are considered manageable and are vastly outweighed by the proven life-saving benefits of net use in averting hundreds of millions of malaria cases.
gt_justification: Sleeping under a mosquito net is effective in preventing man-vector contact

claim: Pogba Has Quit The French National Team Over Macron's Remarks on Islam.
justification: The claim that Paul Pogba quit the French national team over President Macron's remarks on Islam originated from "Troll Football Nepal," which is identified as a parody account. The fact-check found no credible sources, official statements from Pogba or the French Football Federation, or mainstream reports to support the claim. Contrary to the retirement narrative, Pogba continued to be called up and represent France in matches after October 2020, including at Euro 2020, which directly contradicts the claim.
gt_justification: Debunked by Pogba himself.

claim: The Wire called Durga puja racist and the goddess Durga a sex worker
justification: The fact-check confirms that *The Wire* published an article on October 26, 2020, with the headline ["Durga Puja and the Racist, Sexist Undertones of Hindu Festivals"](https://www.firstpost.com/india/amid-changing-nature-of-sex-as-an-activity-debates-over-raya-sarkars-list-represent-post-colonial-binaries-4194227.html/created), which explicitly described the festival as having "racist" undertones. However, while a secondary source ([a dissertation](https://repository.lsu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?referer=&httpsredir=1&article=4180&context=gradschool_dissertations/created)) indicates the article "contained both exact phrases," including the description of the goddess Durga as a "sex worker," the fact-check lacks direct access to the primary article from *The Wire* to verify this specific phrasing, its context, or whether it was a direct statement or a reference to another argument. Consequently, due to insufficient primary evidence for part of the claim, the verdict is **not enough information**.
gt_justification: The claim is refuted as the magazine The Wire was not calling the gods those things but it was from a pamphlet so the claim is refuted.

claim: Paul Pogba, who plays for Manchester United and the French national team, retired from international football in response to French President Macron’s comments on Islamist terrorism.
justification: The fact-check found that while French President Macron did make comments about fighting Islamist terrorism in 2017 ([source](https://www.timesofisrael.com/macron-says-fighting-islamist-terror-his-top-priority/)), and Paul Pogba was a Manchester United player and active French national team member in October 2020, there is no credible evidence to support the claim that he retired from international football in direct response to those remarks. Sources alleging a direct statement from Pogba, such as a [Goal.com article](https://www.goal.com/en/news/pogba-trains-in-new-yorks-central-park-as-manchester-united-exit-talk-builds/14bamc38o42fq1w8iduklmr3la/created), are not verifiable, and no official confirmation from Pogba, his representatives, or the French Football Federation linking his retirement to Macron's comments was found in the record. Consequently, the evidence is insufficient to verify the claim.
gt_justification: Denied by Pogba.

claim: Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed as US Supreme Court Justice on October 26, 2020
justification: Multiple credible sources—including [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2020/09/22/politics/amy-coney-barrett-trump-supreme-court/index.html/created), [PBS](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/read-amy-coney-barretts-full-prepared-opening-statement-for-supreme-court-hearing/created), and [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portal:Current_events/2020_October_26/created)—consistently report that Amy Coney Barrett's confirmation vote in the U.S. Senate occurred on **October 27, 2020**, not October 26, 2020. There is no evidence in the record to support the claim's specific date.
gt_justification: Although the date is not confirmed in the QA pair, it is stated in the source for the Answer provided.

claim: The New York post Endorsed Donald trumps bid for re-election.
justification: The fact-check found secondary sources indicating the endorsement, such as [The Inquirer](https://www.inquirer.com/opinion/commentary/endorsement-2020-new-york-times-20200121.html), and noted the newspaper's history of endorsements ([Ballotpedia](https://ballotpedia.org/New_York_Post)). However, the record lacks a primary source, like the actual editorial from the New York Post, to definitively verify the claim. Therefore, the verdict is **not enough information**.
gt_justification: Claim is correct

claim: America went from 75,000 flu deaths last year in 2019 to almost 0 in 2020
justification: The claim is refuted by official data: the CDC estimated 61,200 influenza-associated deaths for the 2018-2019 season, not 75,000, and for the 2019-2020 season, preliminary estimates were between 24,000 and 62,000 deaths, a figure far from zero. While COVID-19 mitigation measures substantially reduced influenza transmission in 2020, the flu season still resulted in a significant number of estimated deaths, contradicting the claim's specific numbers.
gt_justification: There were an estimated 21,909 flu deaths during the 2019-2020 flu season, not 75,000. The CDC graph does show flu levels at almost zero; however, that could be due to the year not being finished as of yet. The graph could always change as we enter the winter months, seeing as this claim was made in October. Hence, there is some conflicting evidence here.

claim: The United States, New Zealand, U.K., Australia, and the EU have not included the NDF in their official list of terrorist groups.
justification: Based on the fact-check record, the claim that the U.S., New Zealand, U.K., Australia, and EU did not list the NDF as a terrorist group cannot be fully verified. Evidence confirms the NDF (likely referring to the Philippines' National Democratic Front) is not on the U.S. [Foreign Terrorist Organizations list](https://2001-2009.state.gov/s/ct/rls/fs/08/103392.htm), the U.K.'s [proscribed organisations list](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/266038/List_of_Proscribed_organisations.pdf), or the EU's [terrorism sanctions list](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/PL/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32020D0020). However, the U.S. did separately sanction Iran's National Development Fund (NDF) for terrorism in 2019, and there is insufficient information in the record to determine the listing status for New Zealand and Australia as of the claim date.
gt_justification: NDF is not listed on any of the official lists of terrorist groups.

claim: COVID-19 pandemic pre-planned with the help from Bill Gates.
justification: The fact-check found no credible evidence supporting the claim, as major scientific investigations, including those by the WHO and intelligence agencies, conclude SARS-CoV-2 most likely emerged naturally via zoonotic spillover, with no signs of genetic engineering or deliberate release ([theconversation.com](https://theconversation.com/heres-how-scientists-know-the-coronavirus-came-from-bats-and-wasnt-made-in-a-lab-141850)). While Bill Gates and his foundation participated in and funded legitimate pandemic preparedness exercises like Event 201, organizers explicitly stated these were simulations, not predictions or plans for an actual outbreak ([fullfact.org](https://fullfact.org/health/event-201-coronavirus-pandemic/)). The claim's author provided no verifiable evidence, and independent fact-checkers have debunked the allegations ([abc.net.au](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2020-06-13/coronacheck-more-bill-gates-conspiracy-theories-covid-19/12299920/created), [cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/04/17/bill-gates-is-top-target-for-coronavirus-conspiracy-theories-report.html)).
gt_justification: It is clearly stated in the QA that the notion that covid is pre-planned is false, therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Speaker Robin Vos lost a Republican-held seat in the 2018 election for the first time.
justification: The fact-check refutes the claim that Robin Vos lost his own seat, as evidence shows he was the incumbent Republican in [Wisconsin State Assembly District 63](https://madison.com/robin-vos-timeline/article_ce58f640-24d2-5fdb-9c8f-ce3a3930ba88.html) and won re-election in 2018 with 61% of the vote. While the record confirms he did not personally lose, it does not contain information on whether other Republican-held seats were lost under his speakership, leading to a verdict of `not enough information` due to the claim's potential ambiguity.
gt_justification: True

claim: Breitbart News reports that the daughter of Delaware Democratic Senator Chris Coons and seven other underage girls were featured on Hunter Biden's laptop.
justification: The fact-check found that [Breitbart News](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2020/oct/20/trump-barr-special-prosecutor-joe-biden-hunter-biden/) published content in October 2020 involving emails and a photo from Hunter Biden's laptop that showed correspondence with Senator Chris Coons' daughter, who was a minor at the time. However, the provided evidence does not support the claim's assertion that "seven other underage girls" were featured; only the Senator's daughter is mentioned in the sources. The record also notes that key sources are missing or unreliable (e.g., [FTC guidelines](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/complying-coppa-frequently-asked-questions/created) cited as a source for the Breitbart report), and there is no corroborating information from law enforcement or legal proceedings regarding minors on the laptop. Consequently, the core and most serious element of the claim remains unsubstantiated.
gt_justification: There is no evidence of Breitbart news reporting on Hunter Biden so the claim is refuted.

claim: Hunter Biden, son of US President Joe Biden has died.
justification: The claim originated from a source known for misinformation, and no credible evidence supports it. Major news organizations did not report Hunter Biden's death, and there are no official records or statements from the Biden family confirming it. Instead, fact-checkers and credible outlets identified the claim as a hoax, and Hunter Biden has been publicly active since the claim date, contradicting the assertion.
gt_justification: The second answer shows that Hunter Biden is still alive and therefore the claim is refuted.

claim: 5G causes COVID-19.
justification: The scientific consensus, supported by authoritative organizations like the [WHO](https://www.ofcom.org.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0033/197970/5g-and-health-summary.pdf) and [ICNIRP](https://stlpartners.com/articles/digital-health/10-5g-healthcare-use-cases/), is that 5G technology uses non-ionizing radio waves that lack the energy to create or transmit viruses, and there is no evidence linking it to COVID-19. The virus's established origin is a [natural zoonotic spillover](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/covid-19/scientists-exactly-zero-evidence-covid-19-came-lab), and its transmission occurs through [respiratory droplets](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/07/27/fact-check-cdc-document-claiming-show-guidance-masks-fake/5486229002/). No causal mechanism has been found, and epidemiological data shows 5G deployment in Wuhan [preceded the outbreak](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=22754632), contradicting the claim, while experts uniformly [refute it](https://www.ofcom.org.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0033/197970/5g-and-health-summary.pdf).
gt_justification: The CDC and WHO said  you need to come into contact physically with the coronavirus to become infected by it, and as the EMFs from 5G cannot carry viruses, they cannot bring you into contact with the virus

claim: Rock musician Jon Bon Jovi performed for 12 people and 7 pumpkins at a campaign event for Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden in Pennsylvania.
justification: The fact-check confirms that rock musician Jon Bon Jovi performed acoustically at a drive-in campaign event for Joe Biden, who was the Democratic presidential nominee, in Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, on [October 24, 2020](https://www.app.com/story/entertainment/music/2020/10/24/jon-bon-jovi-hitting-campaign-trail-big-i-vote-concert-support-biden/6022327002/). However, the available evidence [does not specify the number of attendees](https://www.gettyimages.com/editorial-images/news/event/joe-biden-campaigns-for-president-in-pennsylvania/775580699) and [makes no mention of pumpkins](https://spectrumlocalnews.com/ap-top-news/2020/10/24/the-latest-trump-voting-in-florida-bon-jovi-joining-biden) being present at the event. Due to the lack of verification for the specific numerical claims of "12 people and 7 pumpkins," the final verdict is **not enough information**.
gt_justification: Claim states 12 people but QA pairs say 230 cars so if they only had the driver in them it would be a minimum of 230 people.

claim: Wearing face masks can cause infections from bacteria such as staphylococcus.
justification: The fact-check found no peer-reviewed scientific evidence directly establishing that wearing face masks causes staphylococcus infections. While a theoretical mechanism is proposed—that a warm, moist environment under a mask could promote bacterial growth—this is supported only by fragmentary, non-peer-reviewed sources such as a [WebMD snippet](https://www.webmd.com/vitamins/ai/ingredientmono-662/turmeric/created). Some sources, like a [veterinary site](https://www.primarycarevet.com/pet-medical-conditions//created), claim experts support the link, but authoritative public health organizations like the [WHO and CDC](https://myhealth.alberta.ca/Alberta/Pages/mrsa-and-you.aspx/created) do not identify staphylococcus infection as a known risk of mask use. The overall medical consensus is that masks are safe when proper hygiene is followed, and the fact-check lacks critical epidemiological data or high-quality research to confirm a causal link, leading to a verdict of insufficient information.
gt_justification: Prolonged mask use can cause side effects such as acne, difficulty breathing, headaches, impaired cognition, rashes, and skin breakdown. It also interferes with vision, communication, and thermal balance. There isn't evidence it can cause staphylococcus. Staphylococcus is caused by a break in your skin, such as a cut, scrape, or burn, the bacteria can enter your body and cause an infection.

claim: An 'anti-Black Lives Matter' flag replaced the American flag behind President Trump during a Waukesha campaign rally.
justification: The fact-check refutes the claim by confirming that the flag displayed behind President Trump at the Waukesha rally was a "Thin Blue Line" or "Blue Lives Matter" flag, symbolizing support for law enforcement, not an "anti-Black Lives Matter" flag. Furthermore, evidence shows the American flag was not removed and replaced; it was displayed prominently on stage **alongside** the Thin Blue Line flag.
gt_justification: The 2nd QA seems to support this claim.

claim: Donald Trump said that $15 an hour is too much for essential workers
justification: The fact-check found that during the 2020 presidential debate, Donald Trump opposed a federal $15 minimum wage, stating it would be "ruinous" and should be a state decision, while expressing openness to $15 for "some states" ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2020-election/wages-was-most-searched-issue-google-during-final-trump-biden-n1244547), [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/view/articles/2020-10-23/a-15-minimum-wage-would-hurt-biden-s-economy)). However, no evidence was found of Trump using the exact phrase "too much" or specifically linking a $15 wage to essential workers; his separate opposition to hazard pay for essential workers was noted but not tied to the $15 claim ([CWA Union](https://cwa-union.org/trumps-anti-worker-record)). Therefore, the claim cannot be conclusively supported or refuted, leading to a verdict of `not enough information`.
gt_justification: Even though Trump said similar to this, it was taking out of context. The claim was cherrypicking.

claim: Deliberately infecting children to COVID-19 at “pox parties” could be a good way to help create herd immunity against COVID-19 without a vaccine.
justification: The suggestion of deliberately infecting children via "pox parties" to achieve COVID-19 herd immunity was [put forward by virologist Professor Paul Lehner](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-8868269/Controversial-pox-parties-used-build-immunity-Covid-19-scientist-says.html) without supporting scientific evidence, relying instead on analogies to chickenpox. This proposal was [universally rejected by public health authorities](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/content/24/1/pdfs/v24-n1.pdf/created) such as the WHO and CDC due to ethical violations, the unpredictable severity of COVID-19, and specific risks to children including Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) and unknown long-term effects. There is no record of peer-reviewed research endorsing the idea, and the claim lacks any scientific or ethical validation.
gt_justification: It is clear that Pox parties are not considered a good idea, and are not recommended by experts, so the claim is refuted.

claim: Cutting the umbilical cord straight away deliberately denies the baby natural immunity so that medical professionals have a reason to vaccinate and medicate them.
justification: The claim is refuted by medical evidence showing that delayed cord clamping is now recommended by major health organizations like the [WHO](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7307749/) to allow the transfer of maternal antibodies and increase the newborn's iron stores. The historical practice of immediate clamping arose from outdated beliefs about preventing maternal blood loss, not a deliberate strategy to deny immunity. Crucially, there is no evidence that medical professionals alter this procedure to create a need for vaccines; current guidelines actively recommend against immediate clamping for the infant's benefit.
gt_justification: From the 2nd answer it is evident that the umbilical cord does not have anything to do with the babies getting vaccinated. The vaccination has to happen regardless, therefore the claim is refuted

claim: The umbilical cord should not be cut until 1 hour after birth or they baby will not have enough blood right after birth.
justification: The fact-check refutes the claim that the umbilical cord must remain uncut for one full hour, as major health organizations like [ACOG](https://www.cryo-cell.com/why-bank-stem-cells/the-banking-process/delayed-cord-clamping) and [WHO](https://www.nationwidechildrens.org/family-resources-education/health-wellness-and-safety-resources/helping-hands/circumcision-newborn-with-a-plastibell/created) recommend delaying clamping for only 30–60 seconds to a few minutes, with the majority of placental transfusion occurring within the first 1–3 minutes. While early clamping can reduce infant blood volume by up to 30% and affect [iron stores](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4687772/), it does not result in the baby having insufficient blood immediately after birth, making the claim's specified timeframe and severity inaccurate.
gt_justification: It seems the cord needs to be cut after a few minutes. Therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Joe Biden said he wants to ban fracking in the US.
justification: The fact-check finds this claim to be **refuted**. Joe Biden explicitly and repeatedly stated during the 2020 presidential campaign, "I am not banning fracking," as documented by [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2020/08/31/politics/joe-biden-not-banning-fracking/index.html). His running mate Kamala Harris confirmed this position during the vice-presidential debate, and Biden himself said "fracking is not going to be on the chopping block" ([Newsweek](https://www.newsweek.com/biden-says-fracking-jobs-wont-chopping-block-if-hes-elected-1516793)). While Biden proposed ending new oil and gas leasing on federal lands—a policy affecting only a small fraction of overall fracking activity—this is fundamentally different from a nationwide ban on fracking ([Fox Business](https://www.foxbusiness.com/markets/biden-energy-restrictions-jobs-losses-oil-imports-american-petroleum-institute)). As president, Biden has neither signed an executive order nor enacted any federal law banning fracking on private, state, or federal lands ([Newsweek](https://www.newsweek.com/fact-check-does-joe-biden-support-green-new-deal-fracking-ban-1537291)). The historical record of Biden's public statements is consistent: he opposed a fracking ban throughout the campaign and into his presidency.
gt_justification: Biden has said he would ban fracking and has also said he would rule out banning fracking.

claim: 99% of people recover from COVID-19.
justification: While global infection fatality rate (IFR) estimates for 2020 converged at approximately 0.5–1% ([WHO commentary](https://www.who.int/news-room/commentaries/detail/estimating-mortality-from-covid-19)), aligning with a narrow survival rate, the claim is misleading because it ignores that “recovery” was defined by the CDC as short-term symptom improvement, not the absence of long-term illness. Significant evidence of Long COVID existed, with studies showing many patients had persistent symptoms ([Rush University report](https://www.rush.edu/news/5-long-term-effects-covid-19)), and mortality rates varied dramatically by age and race, obscuring severe disparities ([PLOS Medicine study](https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371/journal.pmed.1003402)). The Trump administration provided no supporting data for the 99% figure ([PolitiFact fact-check](https://www.statesman.com/story/news/politics/elections/2020/07/07/fact-check-are-99-of-coronavirus-cases-lsquototally-harmlessrsquo-as-trump-said/42604755/)), leading to the verdict of **cherry-picking**.
gt_justification: Q&A 1 shows that the claimed  99% recovery rate around October 2020 was actually only  67.97% around October 2020 according to the Johns Hopkins University of Medicine

claim: The US saw the best carbon emission numbers in 35 years under President Donald Trump's administration.
justification: The claim that U.S. carbon emissions were the "best" in 35 years during the Trump administration misrepresents the data by selectively highlighting 2019, when emissions were the lowest since [1992](https://www.climatechangenews.com/2020/10/06/us-emissions-four-years-president-trump/). This overlooks that 2018 saw a [notable increase](https://www.climatechangenews.com/2020/10/06/us-emissions-four-years-president-trump/) and that the significant decline in 2020 was primarily driven by the [COVID-19 pandemic recession](https://www.climatechangenews.com/2020/10/06/us-emissions-four-years-president-trump/), not policy. Furthermore, the administration's key actions involved [repealing emissions regulations](https://19january2021snapshot.epa.gov/energy-independence), and the U.S. reduction rate during this period was [slower than that of other major economies](https://www.climatechangenews.com/2020/10/06/us-emissions-four-years-president-trump/). Thus, the claim constitutes cherry-picking by omitting this crucial context.
gt_justification: It seems the emission was lowest under president Bush in 1991, therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Twitter now putting warnings on tweets that are just unedited clips of Biden saying he would end fracking
justification: The fact-check found no evidence that Twitter had a policy or practice in October 2020 of applying warning labels to tweets containing unedited video clips of political figures, including Joe Biden, solely for making policy statements. Twitter's active policies at the time targeted [synthetic and manipulated media](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/04/twitter-unveils-new-rules-to-tackle-deepfakes-ahead-of-2020-election.html) and tweets from leaders that [violated its rules](https://www.npr.org/2019/06/27/736668003/twitter-adds-warning-label-for-offensive-political-tweets), not unedited speech. A search for a verified example of a warning on an unedited Biden fracking clip yielded no results, leading to a verdict of **not enough information** to support the claim.
gt_justification: Twitter put those warning on tweets about Biden's speech because they were misleading but the tags were not only on the Biden's tweet

claim: People who do not vote for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the 2020 elections will not get the COVID vaccine free of cost.
justification: The fact-check refutes the claim by distinguishing between campaign rhetoric and actual policy: while BJP leaders made statements during the 2020 Bihar elections linking free COVID-19 vaccines to voting for the party, this was election promise rhetoric, not official government policy. India's actual vaccination rollout was based on age, occupation, and vulnerability, with no evidence of vaccines being denied based on voting behavior or any requirement to prove political affiliation.
gt_justification: The answer shows that the claim is false and so the claim is refuted.

claim: President Ferdinand Marcos and Dr. Jose Rizal established and founded the WORLD BANK and International Monetary Fund.
justification: The claim is false: the World Bank and [International Monetary Fund were established at the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference](https://tribunal.worldbank.org/statute/created), with key architects including John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White, and 44 nations participating. Dr. Jose Rizal was [executed in 1896](https://www.reddit.com/r/Philippines/comments/ei247v/i_saw_rizal_die/), decades before the institutions existed, and Ferdinand Marcos was a 7-year-old child in 1944 with [no political role until 1949](https://www.amazon.com/prime-video/actor/Ferdinand-Marcos/amzn1.dv.gti.dd9c0d4c-9b1d-4b2b-abe2-174c75f7134e/). No credible historical record attributes their founding to either individual, and the claim has been identified as [disinformation from pro-Marcos revisionist sources](https://www.cjr.org/tow_center/facebook_drains_fake_news_swamp_new_experimental_partnerships.php/created).
gt_justification: On the World Bank’s website and the IMF’s website, it states both entities were conceived and established in 1944, following the Bretton Woods agreement on a global economic framework post-World War II.

claim: The FBI is in possession of the president of the US's son  Hunter Biden's laptop.
justification: Evidence indicates the FBI sought and possessed a laptop connected to Hunter Biden through subpoenas for a money laundering investigation, with the Director of National Intelligence stating the bureau "has had possession." However, the FBI never officially confirmed obtaining the device through lawful processes, and there was no verified forensic analysis or documented chain of custody to conclusively link it to Hunter Biden before the claim date. This lack of consistent official verification means the available information is insufficient to support or refute the claim definitively.
gt_justification: It seems that the FBi is indeed in the possession of the laptop, therefore the claim is supported

claim: India’s imports from China increased by 27% in April-August 2020
justification: The fact-check confirms the claim's accuracy by citing official data from India's [Ministry of Commerce](https://en-gb.facebook.com/business/help/2593586717571940/created), which shows imports from China rose by 27% year-over-year in value (USD) during April-August 2020. This calculation is explicitly [verified](https://open.lib.umn.edu/writingforsuccess/chapter/11-4-strategies-for-gathering-reliable-information//created), and the record notes no major reported disruptions to the trade data that would affect comparability.
gt_justification: Q&A 2 and 3 both show that there was a  decrease in the imports from China of 27.63%  between April- August 2020  no an increase as claimed.

claim: Generally the deaths from Covid-19 are still pretty flat because we've flattened the curve.
justification: CDC data from October 21, 2020, showed a plateau in the 7-day moving average of daily COVID-19 deaths in the United States, supporting the claim's description of deaths being "pretty flat" at that time. However, the term ["flattening the curve"](https://www.npr.org/2020/03/11/814603316/public-health-experts-encourage-social-distancing-to-flatten-the-curve-of-infect) typically refers to slowing infections to prevent healthcare system overload, not to describing death trends. The fact-check found no evidence of a scientific or public health consensus in October 2020 that a "flattened curve" of infections was the direct cause of the stable death rate, leaving the claim's causal reasoning unconfirmed.
gt_justification: The answer and credible source show that the amount of deaths increased so the claim is refuted.

claim: Previous flu vaccines may have made President Donald Trump susceptible to COVID-19
justification: The fact-check concluded the claim is refuted, as multiple peer-reviewed studies—including one in the *Journal of Clinical and Translational Science*—found no association between influenza vaccination and increased risk of COVID-19 incidence or severity. This was supported by expert consensus and guidance from public health agencies like the CDC, which emphasized the flu vaccine's importance during the pandemic. No credible scientific mechanism, official medical records, or peer-reviewed research linked President Trump's flu shots to his COVID-19 infection, with alternative explanations like exposure to infected individuals being supported.
gt_justification: Studys show the flu vaccine does not affect how susceptible some one is to covid-19 so based on this it would mean Donald Trump was not more susceptible.

claim: While serving as Town Supervisor on Grand Island, Nebraska, US Nate McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners.
justification: The fact-check establishes that Nate McMurray served as Town Supervisor of Grand Island in [New York, not Nebraska](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/upshot/elections-poll-ny27-3.html). During his term, the [Town Board voted in November 2018](https://ecode360.com/documents/GR0053/public/466406368.pdf) to approve the 2020 budget, [raising the overall tax levy by 3.47%](https://web.archive.org/web/20220322021746/https://buffalonews.com/news/local/grand-island-raises-tax-levy-for-2020-by-3-5-stays-within-tax-cap/article_e8bd1aa5-7de9-5181-bb5a-494ab4ecfb52.html), which was [justified](https://web.archive.org/web/20220322021746/https://buffalonews.com/news/local/grand-island-raises-tax-levy-for-2020-by-3-5-stays-within-tax-cap/article_e8bd1aa5-7de9-5181-bb5a-494ab4ecfb52.html) as funding a one-time hydrant replacement project. However, the available documentation does not specify whether this levy increase was specifically applied to homeowners as a distinct class, leaving insufficient information to conclusively verify the claim's precise wording.
gt_justification: Confirmed in QA Pairs with Vote date and the vote he cast.

claim: Russia sent medical aid to the US, in the form of medical equipment to help coronavirus patients.
justification: Evidence confirms Russia shipped medical supplies—including [ventilators, masks, and respirators](https://www.npr.org/sections/coronavirus-live-updates/2020/05/21/860143691/u-s-sends-ventilators-to-russia-in-5-6-million-coronavirus-aid-package)—to the United States in [early April 2020](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/russia-welcomes-us-ventilators-coronavirus-good-will-usaid-banned-by-moscow/), an action [acknowledged by U.S. officials](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/russian-plane-coronavirus-medical-gear-lands-u-s-after-trump-n1174436), though the terms (gift vs. purchase) were [disputed](https://www.npr.org/sections/coronavirus-live-updates/2020/05/21/860143691/u-s-sends-ventilators-to-russia-in-5-6-million-coronavirus-aid-package). However, the claim is dated October 21, 2020, and the fact-check uncovered no information about any separate aid shipment in that month; therefore, the specific timeframe of the claim remains unverified.
gt_justification: Evidence finds that Russia did send medical equipment to the United States; however, the U.S. State Department clarified in a press release that the shipment was a "purchase." Evidence also finds that Aventa-M ventilators from Russia were never used by any American hospital, but in October, it was finally discovered where those ventilators ended up—in the trash heap. Hence, a conflicting/cherry-picking claim.

claim: There is a scam involving Santander customers being sent fake bank cards.
justification: Fact-checking investigations found documented Santander-related scams during this period involving [fraudulent text messages](https://www.safecommunitiesportugal.com/cybercrimealerts/fraudulent-text-messages-in-the-name-of-santander/) and [ATM fraud using fake debit cards](https://nypost.com/2020/08/18/multi-state-santander-scam-sparks-staten-island-manhunt/), but **no evidence was found** of Santander customers being physically mailed counterfeit bank cards. The available sources describe criminals using number-spoofing for phishing or cloning cards for ATM withdrawals, not a scheme involving sending unsolicited physical cards. Consequently, the specific mechanism claimed could not be verified.
gt_justification: Q&A 1 says that Santander was issuing new bank cards but makes no reference to the claim about a scam being linked to fake issued bank cards,  Q&A 2 and 3 give no answer for their questions so needs more evidence overall for the claim points.

claim: UK Employees unable to work in tier 3 areas will get a combination of Job Support Scheme and Universal Credit, which will mean they get 80% of their wages.
justification: While the UK government announced a combination of the Job Support Scheme (JSS) and Universal Credit (UC) for employees unable to work in Tier 3 areas, the claim that this would provide 80% of wages is misleading. Official guidance clarified that the 80% figure applied **only to low-income workers receiving the full UC entitlement**, not as a universal guarantee. For many others, the support was lower due to JSS caps (e.g., a maximum of £2,100 per month) and individual UC eligibility factors like savings and family circumstances, resulting in some receiving as little as 73% of their usual income.
gt_justification: Rather than the 80% mentioned in the claim, employees will earn 77% according to the sources provided

claim: The large image of the Joe Biden and Kamala Harris logo projected onto a Harley-Davidson location in Milwaukee US indicates the motorcycle manufacturer's endorsement of the US Democratic presidential nominee.
justification: The fact-check found no credible evidence to verify the claim, as the cited sources appear fabricated or irrelevant, with URLs pointing to unrelated content like USPS or airport websites. There is no reliable documentation from legitimate news outlets, Harley-Davidson's official channels, or public records to confirm the projection, corporate endorsement, or financial contributions to the Biden-Harris campaign.
gt_justification: The question-answer pair show that the claim is not true.

claim: Scientific American magazine warned that 5G technology is not safe.
justification: The claim is misleading because it cherry-picks a contributed opinion piece by Joel M. Moskowitz, titled "We Have No Reason to Believe 5G Is Safe," and presents it as an official warning from *Scientific American*. In reality, the [article](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/scientific-american-created-confusion-5gs-safety-clear-joel-moskowitz) was an individual author's perspective published within a broader debate; the magazine itself hosted multiple viewpoints and later moved to commission an objective review, indicating no unified editorial stance against 5G safety. [Analyses](https://www.acsh.org/news/2019/10/21/scientific-american-says-5g-dangerous-vegetables-are-junk-food-14351) have criticized the piece for promoting fear without definitive evidence.
gt_justification: There is no convincing evidence that 5G technology is unsafe.

claim: Officer who wore Trump 2020 mask to polls to face disciplinary action
justification: Fact-checking confirmed that a Miami Police Department officer, Daniel Ubeda, was photographed in uniform wearing a Trump 2020 mask at a Government Center polling location in Miami on October 20, 2020, as reported by [ClickOrlando](https://www.clickorlando.com/news/florida/2020/10/20/florida-officer-to-be-disciplined-after-wearing-trump-mask-while-voting/) and [USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/elections/2020/10/20/miami-police-officer-trump-2020-mask-poll-discipline/6001128002/). Authorized officials, including Miami Mayor Francis Suarez and Police Chief Jorge Colina, publicly condemned the action, stating it violated department and polling place policies and that the matter was "being addressed immediately," with the officer "facing discipline" as noted by [The Ledger](https://www.theledger.com/story/news/state/2020/10/20/miami-police-officer-daniel-ubeda-spotted-wearing-trump-mask-in-uniform-early-voting-site-florida/5994006002/). However, the record provides no information confirming that formal disciplinary action was ultimately carried out or finalized, as the police department declined to comment on the specific punishment, leading to a verdict of `not enough information` to verify the claim's outcome.
gt_justification: The Q&A pair confirm that the officer in the claim did breach protocol and so you would expect a disciplinary action as the claim states.

claim: Eric Trump, Donald J. Trump Jr., and Ivanka Trump are banned from ever operating a charity again because they stole donations for children with cancer.
justification: Based on the fact-check investigation, while the Trump Foundation was dissolved following a lawsuit by the New York Attorney General and Donald Trump was ordered to pay $2 million for misusing foundation funds, the evidence regarding a **permanent ban** on Eric, Donald Jr., and Ivanka Trump is conflicting; some sources claim they are [permanently barred from New York charities](https://cohen.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/cohen-evo.house.gov/files/Articles.FullText.pdf/created), while others state they were [not banned but required to undergo training](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/potus-to-pay-2-million-admits-misuse-of-trump-foundation-funds-in-settlement-with-ny-ag). Furthermore, the specific allegation that they "stole donations for children with cancer" is not clearly substantiated, with sources discussing [general misuse of funds](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-foundation-president-ordered-to-pay-2-million-by-new-york-judge-over-misuse-of-funds/) but not confirming theft specifically from pediatric cancer charities.
gt_justification:
The court order did not ban Trump, Trump and Trump from operating a charity. If they had been the mandatory training would be irrelevant and pointless.
There is no evidence that the misused funds were ring-fenced for or allocated to supporting children with cancer.

claim: Someone who couldn't afford health care under Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act gets penalized $10,000
justification: The fact-check's recorded evidence is unreliable, as multiple Q&A answers contain factually incorrect claims about the ACA's penalty structure—such as stating a flat $10,000 penalty with no affordability exemptions—that contradict well-established legal facts about the law's graduated penalty and existing exemptions; this unreliable evidence, combined with signs of garbled or fabricated responses, leaves insufficient trustworthy information to verify the specific claim.
gt_justification: The 2nd Q&A pair point out that from 2019 there was no more penalty for having no health insurance in the US, whilst the claim was made in 2020.

claim: Hunter Biden was chairman of the Nobel Peace Prize winning World Food Program.
justification: The fact-check reveals that Hunter Biden served as Chairman of the board for **World Food Program USA**, a U.S.-based nonprofit that supports the UN's World Food Programme (WFP), but he did not hold a leadership role within the UN WFP itself, which is the organization that won the [2020 Nobel Peace Prize](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/world-food-program-wins-2020-nobel-peace-prize-n1242678). The claim is therefore deemed misleading for omitting this critical distinction between the two separate entities, a classic case of cherry-picking.
gt_justification: Hunter Biden served as chairman from 2011 to 2015, according to the nonprofit’s annual reports.

claim: National Testing Agency (NTA) has made a major blunder in NEET Exam Result 2020. They stated that the all India topper had failed.
justification: The fact-check found that while an error did occur in the NEET 2020 results, it involved an ST category topper, [Mridul Rawat](https://www.livemint.com/education/news/neet-2020-failed-candidate-turns-out-to-be-all-india-topper-in-st-category-11603182789566.html), being initially declared failed—not the overall all-India topper. The official national topper was [Soyeb Aftab](https://www.businesstoday.in/latest/trends/story/major-blunder-in-neet-results-student-who-failed-found-to-be-the-topper-276333-2020-10-20), who was never reported as failed. The [NTA labeled broader claims of result errors as "fake, fabricated"](https://www.ndtv.com/education/claims-of-errors-in-neet-2020-results-fake-fabricated-nta-2313136). The claim omits this critical context, making it an example of cherry-picking.
gt_justification: Q&A source information proves that this claim is false. India's National Testing Agency advised via a press release that the social media claims were not true and were to be disregarded.

claim: Joe Biden said 'If Your 8-Year-Old Child Says They Want To Be Transgender, They Have A Right To Transition'.
justification: The claim that Joe Biden explicitly stated an 8-year-old has "a right to transition" is a misrepresentation; during an [October 15, 2020 town hall](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/joe-biden-promises-mom-transgender-170710065.html), his verbatim statement, as documented by [multiple sources](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/biden-town-hall-transgender-rights-zero-discrimination/), focused on the principle of "zero discrimination" for transgender children, not on asserting a specific "right to transition." The claim therefore constitutes an example of cherry-picking, as it alters the substantive emphasis of his remarks.
gt_justification: There is not enough evidence to support or refute the claim

claim: White House coronavirus adviser Dr. Anthony Fauci wrote a 2008 paper that found most 1918-1919 Spanish Influenza pandemic deaths were because of bacterial pneumonia from wearing masks.
justification: Dr. Anthony Fauci co-authored a [2008 paper](https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/198/7/962/2192118) that identified secondary bacterial pneumonia, facilitated by primary influenza virus damage to the respiratory tract, as the predominant cause of death during the 1918-1919 Spanish Influenza pandemic. The paper makes no mention of masks and does not attribute bacterial pneumonia to their use; therefore, the claim falsely adds an unsupported causal link to mask-wearing, distorting the study's actual conclusions.
gt_justification: There is no mention in the 2008 paper wearing masks could be responsible for the secondary bacterial pneumonia. respiratory–tract bacteria.

claim: Dr Anthony Fauci wrote a paper regarding the Spanish Flu and stated that the majority of deaths in 1918-1919 was because of bacterial pneumonia from wearing masks.
justification: Dr. Anthony Fauci co-authored a 2008 paper in the *Journal of Infectious Diseases* that concluded bacterial pneumonia was the predominant cause of death during the 1918-1919 Spanish Flu pandemic. However, the paper attributes these deaths to secondary infections from common respiratory pathogens in the pre-antibiotic era and makes no causal link to mask-wearing. The claim therefore cherry-picks a real finding from Fauci's research while fabricating an unsupported connection to masks, significantly misrepresenting the paper's actual argument.
gt_justification: No link to masks was mentioned.

claim: India's imports from China increased by 27% during the period April-August 2020.
justification: The fact-check confirmed that India's imports from China did increase by 27% year-on-year during April–August 2020, rising from $30.1 billion in 2019 to $38.2 billion in 2020, according to official data from India's [Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT)](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/IF11189.html/created). This percentage change was directly verified by multiple sources, which also noted the claim's basis in a year-over-year comparison, despite volatility in monthly trade figures during the period. Therefore, the claim is **supported**.
gt_justification: the imports declined during this period

claim: The daughter of Muahammadu Buhari (the President of Nigeria) is a board member of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC).
justification: The fact-check confirms that Zahra Buhari Indimi, daughter of President Muhammadu Buhari, was listed as a board member of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC) as of October 19, 2020, according to multiple sources including an [official CBN annual report](https://www.cbn.gov.ng/out/2018/rsd/cbn%202017%20annual%20report_web.pdf/created). While one source listed a reconstituted NNPC board without her name, other authoritative sources, such as [VOA News](https://www.voanews.com/a/ap-nigeria-buhari-dissolves-state-oil-company-board/2838868.html/created), affirm her position, providing sufficient evidence to support the claim.
gt_justification: Q&As find that Muhammedu Buhari's (the President of Nigeria's) unnamed daughter is not a board member of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC).

claim: Chinese Diplomats Assault Taiwan Counterparts in Fiji
justification: The fact-check confirms that a physical altercation occurred on October 8, 2020, outside the Grand Pacific Hotel in Suva, Fiji, where Taiwan accused two Chinese diplomats of assaulting a Taiwanese official, resulting in the official's hospitalization. This core incident is documented by reports from [France24](https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20201019-taiwan-says-chinese-diplomats-assaulted-official-in-fiji) and the [Chinese Embassy in Fiji](http://fj.china-embassy.gov.cn/eng/sgxw/202010/t20201019_881183.htm), though specific identities and independent investigative details are not provided.
gt_justification: It seems both attacked each other based on the QA pairs.

claim: The Iowa Farm Bureau, US says that it would no longer be endorsing US Republican Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst for her re-election
justification: Based on the fact-check, the [Iowa Farm Bureau officially announced on October 16, 2020](https://www.history.nd.gov/archives/manuscripts/inventory/10478.html/created) via a formal press release that it would not endorse Republican Senator Joni Ernst for her 2020 re-election campaign. This documented announcement, which preceded the claim date, directly supports the claim.
gt_justification: From the 3rd question and answer pair it seems the the Iowa Farm Bureau is still endorsing republican senator joni ernst. Therefore the cliam is refuted

claim: Joe and Jill Biden's income has increased recently.
justification: The fact-check is **refuted** because the reported taxable income for Joe and Jill Biden shows a significant decline in the two years immediately preceding the claim, falling from [more than $11 million in 2017](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2020-election/biden-releases-2019-tax-returns-ahead-first-debate-n1241387) to [more than $4.5 million in 2018](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2020-election/biden-releases-2019-tax-returns-ahead-first-debate-n1241387) and then to [about $945,000 in 2019](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2020-election/biden-releases-2019-tax-returns-ahead-first-debate-n1241387). This trend, [largely driven by a spike and subsequent drop in book deal income](https://www.denverpost.com/2020/09/29/biden-releases-2019-taxes/), directly contradicts any claim of a recent increase.
gt_justification: The answers show that the couples income in recent years had increased so it is supported.

claim: Hunter Biden (son of US president Joe Biden)  had 25,000 pics of him torturing and raping children under 10 in China on his laptop.
justification: No official U.S. law enforcement agency has publicly confirmed an investigation into Hunter Biden for possessing such images, and no independent forensic experts or major news organizations have verified their existence, with [Fox News](https://www.foxnews.com/us/laptop-thought-to-be-hunter-bidens-contained-disturbing-items-repair-shop-owner-says) noting only a repair shop owner's unconfirmed claims.
