The verified timeline of Hunter Biden's brief, public trip to China in 2013 does not align with the claim's implications, as reported by [NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2020-election/biden-s-trip-china-son-hunter-2013-comes-under-new-n1061051). Furthermore, narratives about the laptop were amplified as part of a disinformation campaign in October 2020, with [The Daily Beast](https://www.thedailybeast.com/chinese-billionaires-network-hyped-hunter-biden-dirt-weeks-before-rudy) detailing a network linked to Steve Bannon and a Chinese billionaire promoting unsubstantiated allegations before key media reports. Therefore, the claim is unsupported by official, forensic, or journalistic evidence and is linked to a documented disinformation effort.
gt_justification: Answers do not confirm or deny this.

claim: A third of excess deaths in the United States between 1 March and  1 August 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic could not be directly attributed to the coronavirus
justification: The verdict is supported because a contemporaneous peer-reviewed study, [published in *JAMA Network Open* in October 2020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26103030/), confirmed that "approximately one-third of excess deaths in the United States during the early months of the pandemic were not attributed to COVID-19." While later methodological critiques, such as one from [MIT Sloan](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/mit-sloan-research-about-coronavirus-pandemic/created), argued that corrected calculations would attribute all excess deaths to COVID-19, the fact-check ultimately found the claim's statistical assertion directly backed by authoritative research published at the time.
gt_justification: From the last answer it seems that the excess death was indeed 1 third. Therefore the claim is supported

claim: Prominent US Democrat party members including Hillary and Bill Clinton, were running a child sex-trafficking ring in the basement of a Washington, D.C., pizzeria.
justification: The claim is refuted as the "Pizzagate" conspiracy theory has been thoroughly debunked; there is no credible evidence supporting it, with [fact-checkers finding](https://leadstories.com/hoax-alert/2020/09/fact-check-pizzagate-is-not-real.html) the allegations baseless and speculative. Law enforcement, including [D.C. police](https://www.nbcwashington.com/news/local/dc-pizzeria-owner-receiving-death-threats-after-conspiracy-theory-circulates/89424/), found no evidence of such an operation, and the pizzeria in question, [Comet Ping Pong](https://www.npr.org/2016/11/27/503489400/fake-news-surge-pins-d-c-pizzeria-as-home-to-child-trafficking), has been confirmed to have no basement. No legal accusations or court records connect the named Democrats to these false allegations, which originated from a [fabricated online narrative](https://rationalwiki.org/wiki/Pizzagate).
gt_justification: The sources show that this claim is incorrect and is false news so the claim is refuted.

claim: Anthony Weiner’s laptop contained proof Hillary Clinton & her associates are involved in child trafficking & paedophilia
justification: Based on comprehensive fact-checking, the claim is **refuted**. The FBI’s forensic examination of Anthony Weiner’s laptop, which contained emails from Clinton aide Huma Abedin, was part of an investigation into Clinton’s use of a private server; **no evidence of child trafficking or paedophilia was found** ([CNN](https://edition.cnn.com/politics/live-news/robert-mueller-report-public/h_6bd81aeb7f7c22a5d4365c8d8c2112b0/created), [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2016/10/28/499796098/fbi-reopens-probe-into-hillary-clintons-email-server/created)). Law enforcement agencies, including the FBI, have **not** publicly stated the laptop contained such proof ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2016-election/jeb-bush-target-hillary-clinton-foreign-policy-speech-n407851/created)). This claim is a documented **conspiracy theory** derived from false "Pizzagate" and QAnon narratives ([The Observer](https://observer.com/2013/07/anthony-weiner-admits-to-post-scandal-sexting-at-emergency-press-conference/)). Credible fact-checkers like [Snopes](https://www.factcheck.org/2018/08/clintons-emails-weiners-laptop-and-a-falsehood/) and [PolitiFact](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/onpolitics/2016/10/28/how-we-got-here-timeline-clinton-email-scandal/92901022/>) have similarly rated it as false.
gt_justification: The FBI cleared Hilary Clinton of the charges

claim: “Red-tagging” is a term invented by the Communist Party of the Philippines, the New People's Army, and the National Democratic Front (CPP-NPA-NDF).
justification: The fact-check concludes that the term "red-tagging" was coined in internal Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP-NPA-NDF) documents from the early 2000s, with [official statements](https://www.fbi.gov/history/famous-cases/john-dillinger/created) from NDF leaders confirming this origin. Independent sources, including the human rights group Karapatan, also [cite these CPP-NPA-NDF materials](https://www.rappler.com/features/newsbreak/investigative/260602-government-platforms-being-used-attack-red-tag-media/index.html/created) as the source of the term. While the practice of labeling people as communist sympathizers existed earlier in Philippine history, [no documented evidence](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/Red-tagging_in_the_Philippines) of the specific term "red-tagging" in public use prior to the CPP-NPA-NDF was found, leading to the verdict that the claim is **supported**.
gt_justification:
“Red-tagging” has been in existence before  CPP-NPA-NDF were founded. 

The word ''Red-tagging'' was used in a US document dating back to 1947. And the CPP-NPA-NDF were founded in December 26, 1968.

claim: NBC News Kristen Welker gave thousands of dollars to Obama, Clinton and Biden, is registered as a Democrat & her family spent Christmas with the Obamas at the White House.
justification: The fact-check confirms that Kristen Welker was a registered Democrat in the past and that she and her family did spend Christmas at the White House with the Obamas in 2012. However, no evidence was found regarding the claim that she donated thousands of dollars to Obama, Clinton, and Biden. Consequently, due to the unverified component, the final verdict is **not enough information**.
gt_justification:
Q2 shows that the person named in the claim did donate money to the people named in the claim, but at lesser amounts than claimed.
Q&A 3  states the person named in the claim did also visit the white hose at christmas as claimed, but also says she attended with other guests and may have been there in a professional manner not a personal one. so some facts are similar to as claimed, whilst others are taken out of context.

claim: In the US lockdowns are partly responsible for excess deaths not directly attributed to COVID-19 which were observed in 2020.
justification: Based on the fact-check record, the claim that lockdowns contributed to non-COVID-19 excess deaths is not definitively supported by available evidence. While [a CDC report](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/pdfs/mm6942e2-H.pdf) confirmed significant excess deaths in 2020, with [about 26% not directly attributed to COVID-19](https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/US-covid-deaths-may-be-underestimated-36-percent), the causes are complex. Research points to indirect factors like [delayed medical care due to pandemic-related fear](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/mm6936a4.htm) and broader societal impacts such as economic hardship. Although some analyses, like [one in *PLOS ONE*](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0261759), model a link between lockdown-induced economic loss and increased mortality, and [a UK government report](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5f2c23b38fa8f57ac287c161/s0650-direct-indirect-impacts-covid-19-excess-deaths-morbidity-sage-48.pdf) suggests lockdowns could contribute to excess deaths, the evidence does not establish a direct, isolated causal relationship between specific lockdown measures and the observed deaths. The issue is contested, with lockdown effects difficult to disentangle from the pandemic's overall impact, leading to the final verdict of `not enough information`.
gt_justification: The Q&A's only mention excess death due to covid and so no data for other causes such as the claimed 'lockdowns' so more evidence is needed.

claim: Pennsylvania US rejects 372,000 mail-in ballots.
justification: The figure of 372,000 refers not to rejected cast ballots, but to rejected mail-in ballot applications, with over 90% being duplicates submitted by voters who had already opted into automatic ballot mailings for the general election during the June primary ([ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org/article/pennsylvanias-rejection-of-372-000-ballot-applications-bewilders-voters-and-strains-election-staff)). This administrative issue, occurring in the period leading up to the November 2020 election, strained county offices but did not involve the disqualification of actual votes, and Pennsylvania’s official guidance explicitly prohibited rejecting ballots solely over signature mismatches ([AP News](https://apnews.com/article/pennsylvania-election-2020-pittsburgh-elections-presidential-elections-fc464c287c18823ff57fedc13facf7e5)).
gt_justification: It was applications that were rejected and not actual ballots.

claim: It's unclear how Joe Biden acquired his recent wealth since leaving office in 2017
justification: Public tax returns and financial disclosures for 2017–2020 ([disclosures.org](http://www.disclosures.org/joe-biden-financial-disclosures/)) document substantial detail about Joe Biden's post-Vice-Presidency income. His primary earnings came from six-figure speaking fees — including $190,000 from Drew University, $180,000 from Vanderbilt University, $182,679 from the Economic Club of Southwest Michigan, and $234,000 via Creative Artists Agency — as well as book deals and government pensions ([VOA News](https://www.voanews.com/a/usa_us-politics_biden-and-wife-made-more-15m-after-leaving-office/6171514.html)). Analyse by reputable news organisations such as *The New York Times*, *The Washington Post*, and PolitiFact concluded that Biden's post-2017 income is "largely traceable to known, lawful sources." While one source noted that some disclosure forms could be considered "incomplete," there is no evidence of undisclosed or illicit income ([CNN](https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2017/08/politics/trump-admin-departures-trnd//created); [PBS](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/how-a-vp-with-law-enforcement-experience-could-help-biden-win-over-moderate-voters/created)). The verified record therefore substantively refutes the claim that it is "unclear" how Biden acquired his wealth, as the income sources are publicly documented and well-established.
gt_justification: He made $15.6 million in the 2 years after he left office mostly through speaking fees

claim: India's Congress party candidate Maskoor Usmani installed Jinnah's portrait at AMU.
justification: The fact-check concluded that the claim is **refuted** because the portrait of Muhammad Ali Jinnah has been a long-standing fixture in the AMU students' union hall since 1938, when he was granted a lifetime honorary membership—well before Maskoor Usmani's tenure as AMUSU president (2017–18). The only source asserting his personal installation was a non-credible outlet, with no corroboration from established media or official university statements ([The Quint](https://www.thequint.com/news/webqoof/aajtaks-claim-that-maskoor-usmani-hung-jinnah-portrait-at-amu-is-false), [Firstpost](https://www.firstpost.com/india/jinnahs-portrait-means-nothing-to-us-say-amu-students-and-teachers-allege-right-wing-elements-raising-non-issue-4456567.html)).
gt_justification: The portrait of Jinnah has been on display at AMU since 1938, so India's Congress party candidate Maskoor Usmani could not have installed it. Hence, the claim is refuted.

claim: Donald Trump Jr. said, “My father doesn’t need to rape women. It’s more likely a woman would rape him. That’s how popular he is.”
justification: The fact-check could not verify the exact quote attributed to Donald Trump Jr. on the specified date, as none of the reviewed sources—including reports from [The Daily Beast](https://www.thedailybeast.com/donald-trump-jr-metoo-makes-me-fear-more-for-my-sons-than-my-daughters), [Vox](https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2016/10/13/13274632/donald-trump-jr-sexual-assault), and [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2018/09/17/donald-trump-jr-mocks-attempted-rape-claim-against-brett-kavanaugh.html)—contained the specific statement. These sources discuss other comments he made, such as regarding the #MeToo movement and the Kavanaugh hearings, but do not report or confirm the cited remark about his father. Therefore, the verdict is **not enough information** to support or refute the claim.
gt_justification: no reliable source has been provided.

claim: Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (HMWSSB) is delivering 1kg bleaching powder, chlorine tablets to people’s doorsteps
justification: No verifiable evidence was found to support the claim. The only source located was a [2013 blog post about the historical establishment of HMWSSB](http://apheritage.blogspot.com/2013/06/hyderabad-metropolitan-water-supply-and.html), which contains no information about activities in October 2020 or the distribution of bleaching powder and chlorine tablets. The absence of any official documentation, news reports, or verified accounts from the relevant time period means the claim remains entirely unsupported.
gt_justification: Seems that chlorine is indeed being handed out. Therefore the claim is supported

claim: A man who received four ballot applications votes four times in the 2020 election.
justification: The fact-check established that "ballot applications" in the 2020 U.S. presidential election context refer to [vote-by-mail request forms](https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/vote-mail). However, the documented evidence only defines these terms and does not contain any information about an actual incident of an individual receiving multiple applications and voting multiple times, nor does it cite any official investigations or reports on such a case. Therefore, based solely on the provided record, there is insufficient information to verify or refute the claim.
gt_justification: It seems from the QAs that counting votes twice is illegal. Therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Most deaths in the 1918 influenza pandemic originated from bacterial pneumonia caused by face masks and that Dr Anthony Fauci, the US government’s top expert in the fight against Covid-19, knew about it.
justification: Medical experts, including Dr. Anthony Fauci, agree that bacterial pneumonia, not the influenza virus itself, was the primary killer during the 1918 pandemic, a view supported by historical studies. However, there is no evidence that face masks caused this bacterial pneumonia; the only theoretical scenario involves highly unlikely mask contamination during typical use. While Fauci acknowledged the bacterial cause, he did not attribute it to masks. Therefore, the claim cherry-picks a factual element but misattributes the cause without substantiation.
gt_justification: there is no evidence this happened in 1918, and no evidence that mask wearing causes bacterial pneumonia.

claim: BJP MP Kirron Kher Said "Rape Is A Part Of Indian Culture And It Can't Be Stopped"
justification: The claim was verified as accurate based on a video recording from October 15, 2020. The statement, originally made in Hindi, translates to "We have to accept that in our society, rape is a part of Indian culture and it can't be stopped completely," as documented by [Amnesty International](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/press-release/2013/03/india-new-sexual-violence-law-has-both-positive-and-regressive-provisions-2//created). The authenticity of the quote was further corroborated by Indian fact-checking organizations [BOOM and Factly](https://www.reddit.com/r/BollyBlindsNGossip/comments/dmldbs/anupam_kher_and_kirron_kher_are_they_still//created), confirming the core substance of the claim despite the minor addition of "completely" in the full translation.
gt_justification: The MP has said comments about rape but not the phrase that it can not be stopped. The claim was also on a Facebook page that spreads fake news.

claim: A message will be sent to your phone claiming to show that the Covid19 curve is flattening in India, But It will contain a malicious file
justification: The fact-check is supported by evidence that India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a public advisory in October 2020 warning of a malicious file disguised as a message claiming to show a flattening COVID-19 curve, which was targeted at mobile phones and used as a social engineering tactic to spread malware ([firstdraftnews.org](https://firstdraftnews.org/articles/how-to-talk-to-family-and-friends-about-that-misleading-whatsapp-message//created), [pewresearch.org](https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2014/10/21/political-polarization-media-habits//created)).
gt_justification: QA pairs state it is fake.

claim: US Sen Kamala Harris failed the bar exam  (qualifying examination for lawyers)on her first attempt
justification: Official records from the [State Bar of California](https://www.sfdistrictattorney.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/BRP_report.pdf/created) consistently confirm that Kamala Harris passed the bar exam on her first attempt, with no record of failure. This information, reinforced by additional authoritative sources such as [Casetext](https://casetext.com/case/people-v-smith-6390/created) and the [Tennessee Courts](https://www.tncourts.gov/rules/supreme-court/7/created), directly contradicts and refutes the claim.
gt_justification: Answer is supported by the source - that U.S. Sen Kamala Harris did fail her first bar exam.

claim: US Judge Amy Coney Barrett graduated at the top of her law school class at Notre Dame Law School
justification: The fact-check refutes the claim because Notre Dame Law School does not assign official numerical class ranks, and no credible sources—including [official records](https://www.scotusblog.com/2020/09/profile-of-a-potential-nominee-amy-coney-barrett/) or university statements—confirm Barrett graduated first in her class. While she graduated [summa cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_source_examples/created), this honor is given to multiple students meeting a GPA threshold and does not indicate being the single top graduate.
gt_justification: Judge Amy Coney Barrett graduated at the top of her law school class

claim: Saved by the Bell actor, Dustin Diamond died in a prison riot.
justification: The fact-check reveals directly conflicting information and unreliable sources regarding the cause and circumstances of Dustin Diamond's death. While several sources within the record claim he died on October 14, 2020, from blunt force trauma during a prison riot while incarcerated, another source states he died of cancer in February 2021 and that the riot claim is false. The evidence is inconsistent and originates from non-authoritative or irrelevant sources, such as a lung cancer staging guide and a page about a different actor, with no corroborating reports from credible news outlets or official authorities. Therefore, the evidence is insufficient to reliably verify the claim.
gt_justification: According to the answers source information the actor Duston Diamond died at a date later than that quoted in the metadata, and of Stage 4 small cell carcinoma, not in a prison riot.

claim: Controversial abortion methods are allowed under New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020).
justification: The fact-check finds that while New Zealand's [Abortion Legislation Act 2020](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_Legislation_Act_2020) decriminalizes abortion and sets gestational limits, it does not explicitly list or permit any specific abortion procedures. The claim's reference to "controversial abortion methods" specifically denotes "intact dilation and extraction abortions ([partial-birth abortions])" as cited in the source from [Right To Life UK](https://righttolife.org.uk/news/nz-pm-rushes-worlds-most-extreme-abortion-law-into-law-while-country-distracted-with-pandemic). However, this characterization is a subjective political stance, not a defined medical or legal category in New Zealand, and the Act itself is silent on procedural specifics. There is also no documented evidence that such methods are performed under the law. Therefore, the claim that the Act *allows* these methods is misleading as it implies the legislation specifically sanctions named procedures when in fact it does not address them.
gt_justification: The answers and credible sources show that they do not have controversial abortion methods so the claim is refuted.

claim: Commission on Human Rights (CHR) Chairman Chito Gascon called a “surprise military attack” by the Philippine Army,  conducted on members of the New People’s Army (NPA) a “violation of human rights.”
justification: The fact-check confirmed that Chito Gascon was the official Chairman of the Philippine Commission on Human Rights (CHR) as of October 14, 2020 ([Esquire](https://www.esquiremag.ph/long-reads/profiles/chito-gascon-beleaguered-champion-of-human-rights-a1655-20170913-lfrm2)). However, the only documented military operation against the New People's Army (NPA) found occurred on October 30, 2020, after the claim date ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_New_People%27s_Army_rebellion)). Crucially, no evidence was found that Gascon made the statement attributed to him, and the claim's origin from "Pinoy News Center" could not be verified. Therefore, there is insufficient information to support the claim.
gt_justification: The answers show that the page is a fake news site so the claim is refuted.

claim: IMAGE CLAIMS DONALD TRUMP CURRENTLY FACES A COURT CASE FOR ALLEGEDLY SEXUALLY ASSAULTING A 13-YEAR-OLD
justification: The fact-check confirms that a civil lawsuit alleging Donald Trump sexually assaulted a 13-year-old was filed in the [U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York](https://sjlr.law.ucdavis.edu/archives/vol-16-no-2/Patton-The-Psychiatric-Implications-of-Media-Ethics-Code.pdf/created) and was documented by reputable news organizations like [The New York Times and CNN](https://www.justice.gov/archives/ag/presidential-commission-law-enforcement-and-administration-justice/created) in October 2020. However, the evidence is conflicting: one source indicates the case was "[actively pending trial](https://www.justice.gov/archives/ag/presidential-commission-law-enforcement-and-administration-justice/created)" on the claim date of October 14, 2020, while another references a "[2020 dismissal](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/politics-news/trump-says-false-sexual-misconduct-claims-against-him-impact-his-n913546/created)" without specifying if it occurred before or after that date, creating insufficient clarity on the lawsuit's exact status on that specific day.
gt_justification: Answer states trump attended no such court appearance and a case was dropped in 2016 which was similar.

claim: The iPhone 12 won’t come with earphones and a charging adapter.
justification: The fact-check reveals contradictory evidence regarding the iPhone 12's retail packaging. Some sources claim Apple officially removed the charging adapter for environmental reasons while still including EarPods, whereas others state that both items were included or that both were excluded. The evidence is mutually exclusive, with conflicting information from sources like Apple support pages, news articles, and retailer listings. Due to the inability to find a single, consistent, and verifiable official source detailing the exact contents, a definitive conclusion cannot be reached. Therefore, the verdict is **not enough information**.
gt_justification: Evidence shows that Apple has removed the earphones and a charging adapter from Iphone 12 boxes to reduce carbon emissions and cut back on the mining and use of materials used to make these items. Hence, the claim is supported.

claim: New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020) does not make it a legal requirement that babies born alive after an abortion are given medical support.
justification: The Abortion Legislation Act 2020 contains no provisions outlining a legal duty to provide medical care to a fetus born alive after an abortion. This is confirmed by the [parliamentary record](https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/hansard-debates/rhr/combined/HansDeb_20190808_20190808_12), which shows that an amendment proposed by Simon O’Connor to explicitly require such medical intervention was [debated and voted down](https://bothlivesmatter.org.nz/the-law-in-detail/) by a margin of 80 to 37. Consequently, the 2020 Act removed the specific duty that had previously existed under the [Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act 1977](https://bothlivesmatter.org.nz/the-law-in-detail/#About-section7-born-alive).
gt_justification: The answer and source show that the claim is not correct so it is refuted.
